raw_segments.text: In 1262, being the 51st of Henry E.I., was revived an ancient statute, called the Assize
of Bread and Ale, which, the king says in the preamble, had been made in the times of
his progenitors, sometime kings of England.
It is probably, therefore, as old at least as the time of his grandfather, Henry I.,
and may have been as old as the conquest.
It regulates the price of bread according, as the prices of wheat may happen to be, from
one shilling to twenty shillings, the quarter of the money of those times.
But statutes of this kind are generally presumed to provide with equal care for all deviations
from the middle price, for those below it, as well as for those above it.
Ten shillings, therefore, containing six ounces of silver, tower weight, and equal to about
thirty shillings of our present money, must, upon this supposition, have been reckoned
the middle price of the quarter of wheat when this statute was first enacted, and must have
continued to be so in the 51st of Henry E.I.
We cannot, therefore, be very wrong in supposing that the middle price was not less than one-third
of the highest price, at which this statute regulates the price of bread, or than six
